title: LLM optimization: how to structure a page AI can quote
meta_description: LLM optimization at page level, with 2026 data: front-loading answers, chunk-level retrieval, tables and lists, schema, and what the extraction studies show.
og_title: LLM optimization: what the extraction studies actually show
og_description: 44.2% of ChatGPT citations came from the first 30% of a page in one 2026 analysis. Schema showed no major uplift in a controlled test. How to write for extraction.
h1: LLM optimization: how to write and structure a page an engine can lift an answer from
card_summary: How to write and structure a page so an AI engine can lift an answer from it: front-loading, chunk-level retrieval, tables and lists, schema, and a confidence rating on each extraction study.
extract_html: LLM optimization at page level means writing each section so it can be lifted on its own: answer the question in the first sentence, put your strongest claims early, and keep key facts in visible HTML, using tables and lists where the content suits them. In Kevin Indig's 2026 analysis, 44.2% of citations came from the first 30% of a page's text[1]. Schema is weaker than its reputation: a controlled 2026 Ahrefs test of 1,885 pages found no major citation uplift from adding it[9].
body_html:
How do AI engines pull an answer out of a page?

They score passages as well as pages, then hand the best ones to the model. That is chunk-level retrieval. The clearest public description comes from Perplexity, which said in September 2025 that its Search API aims "to decompose documents into self-contained spans, each of which can be individually retrieved and ranked at query time"[3]. Microsoft's Krishna Madhavan described AI assistants in similar terms in October 2025: they "break content into smaller, usable pieces", judge those pieces, then combine them into one reply[4].

The consequence is our inference, not a tested result: a section that only makes sense after the previous three will not survive being pulled out alone. "This approach" and "as mentioned above" point at nothing once the passage leaves your page.

Three limits on what is known:

  • Nobody publishes the chunk size. Perplexity's post gives no sizes or boundary rules[3], and we found no engine that does as of November 2026. Token counts circulate on vendor blogs. We could not trace any of them to an engine's own documentation, so do not write to one.
  • Longer snippets go with citation, but the cause is open. In an October 2026 preprint on production ChatGPT (80 queries, 20 runs each, collected between March and July 2026), 16.5% and 16.9% of cited snippets reached 500 characters or more, against 1.5% and 1.9% of uncited ones, for GPT-5.3 Instant and GPT-5.5 Instant[6]. The study is observational, and longer snippets may simply reflect source type or structure[6].
  • Google says you need not chop anything up. Its guide states "There's no requirement to break your content into tiny pieces", because its systems can "show the relevant piece to users"[5]. That covers Google only, and it still describes showing a piece of a page.

Our reading of both positions: keep normal sections of normal length, and make each one complete. Do not split one good page into twenty thin ones.

Why should the answer come first?

Because citations cluster near the top of a page, and a lifted passage has to make its point without help. Indig reports that "44.2% of all citations originate from the first 30% of the text"[1]. Ahrefs' March 2026 summary of the same work gives the rest: 31.1% from the 30% to 70% stretch and 24.7% from the final section[2]. An even spread would give the opening 30% of citations, so it earns about 1.5 times its share (our arithmetic).

Rate this as moderate evidence. The original post from February 2026 is paywalled, so we read only the preview, and we could not audit the method. Its subtitle says 1.2 million search results, while Ahrefs says 1.2 million ChatGPT citations[1][2]. It is also observational. Writers put summaries at the top, so the pattern may reflect what sits there and not the position itself. Front-loading costs almost nothing either way, so we do it:

  • At page level, open with a standalone answer of under 60 words. The 60 is our house rule, not a tested threshold.
  • At section level, answer the heading in the first sentence, then support it.
  • In every claim, name the subject and attach a number, a year and a source.

The last point has the only controlled support. In the GEO paper (KDD 2024), adding quotations raised position-adjusted word count from a baseline of 19.3 to 27.2, adding statistics raised it to 25.2, and keyword stuffing cut it to 17.7[12]. The test engine ran on gpt3.5-turbo, not a current production model, so treat the size of those gains as directional[12].

What do the extraction studies actually show?

They support clear headings and early answers, give modest support to tables and lists, and find no major uplift from adding schema. The ratings below are our judgement. AirOps and Ahrefs both sell products in this market, and so do we, so weigh all three readings accordingly.

LLM optimization tactics against the best public evidence we could verify (sources checked November 2026). AirOps does not spell out its citation rate denominator.
TacticStudy and sampleResultOur confidence
Answers early on the pageIndig, February 2026, reported as 1.2 million results or citations[1][2]44.2% of citations from the first 30% of textModerate: observational, method paywalled
Headings that match the queryAirOps, April 2026, 16,851 queries, 50,553 ChatGPT responses[7]41.0% citation rate at similarity 0.90 or above, 30.2% below 0.50Moderate: observational, ChatGPT only
Lists and tables togetherSame AirOps data[7]33.9% against 31.0% with neither. Product pages: 37.8% against 24.4%Low overall, moderate for product pages
Tables on comparison contentAirOps, April 2026, 217,508 retrieved pages, 7,500 commercial queries[8]Pages with 3 tables earned 25.7% more citationsLow to moderate: relative lift, no absolute rates
Adding JSON-LD schemaAhrefs, May 2026, 1,885 pages against matched controls[9]AI Overviews -4.6%, AI Mode +2.4%, ChatGPT +2.2%High for already-cited pages, unknown for others
Longer pagesAhrefs, December 2025, 174,048 pages cited in AI Overviews[11]0.04 Spearman correlation between word count and citation positionModerate: AI Overviews only

One finding from the AirOps data belongs beside every row: only 2.3% of page-query combinations were cited in all 3 runs[7]. Testing a rewrite with a single prompt tells you very little, which is why our guide to measuring AI visibility starts with sampling.

Do tables and lists help engines extract your content?

Probably for comparisons and product pages, and only slightly elsewhere. Across all pages in the April 2026 AirOps data, having both lists and tables moved the citation rate by 2.9 points, from 31.0% to 33.9%[7]. On product pages the gap was 13.4 points[7]. In commercial search, pages with 7 to 26 list sections were 6% to 15.2% more likely to earn a citation[8].

Neither report added a table to a page and watched what happened. They compare pages that already differ in many ways. The mechanism is plausible, though: Microsoft says lists, numbered steps and comparison tables "break complex details into clean, reusable segments"[4]. That is guidance from a platform, not a test result.

How we build them:

  • Use a real HTML table with a header row and a caption that states what is being compared and when.
  • Put one fact in each cell, with its unit.
  • Keep core facts out of images and PDFs. Microsoft warns against both, and against hidden content that AI systems may not render[4].
  • Use a table when several things share several attributes. A question with one answer stays a sentence.

Does schema markup help with LLM optimization?

Not measurably for pages already being cited, based on the best controlled test so far. Ahrefs tracked 1,885 pages that added JSON-LD between August 2025 and March 2026, and compared them with matched pages that never did. The authors conclude that "Adding schema produced no major uplift in citations on any platform"[9]. The AI Mode and ChatGPT changes were statistically indistinguishable from zero. The AI Overviews decline was statistically significant, but both groups were already falling and Ahrefs cannot say whether schema caused it[9].

That study also shows why raw comparisons mislead. AI Mode citations rose 43% from before schema was added to after, but the control pages rose almost as much[9]. Keep that in mind when you read AirOps' 38.5% citation rate for pages with JSON-LD against 32.0% without[7]: it has no such control.

Read more: what the Ahrefs test cannot tell you

Every page in the Ahrefs sample had 100 or more AI Overview citations in February 2025, before any schema was added, so the result says nothing about pages AI systems never see. The window was 30 days, schema types were pooled, and only JSON-LD embedded in the HTML was studied[9]. Pages that add schema often change other things at the same time too.

There is also a mechanical reason to keep facts visible. In an October 2025 searchVIU test on one fictional product page with eight variants, no system tested found a price that existed only in JSON-LD, either live or after indexing. ChatGPT and Gemini found the plain HTML price on live fetch, and Google AI Mode found it after indexing[10]. Only Gemini read a JavaScript-rendered price on live fetch. The sample is tiny, and the authors note schema could still be used at the indexing or search stages[10].

Google says structured data isn't required and there is no special markup to add, but advises keeping it for rich results[5]. So keep the schema you have for that reason, and never let it be the only place a fact lives.

Does page length or a separate page per query matter?

Length barely registers, and a page per query variation carries risk. Ahrefs found a 0.04 Spearman correlation between word count and citation position across 174,048 AI Overview pages, and 53.4% of cited pages were under 1,000 words[11]. In the ChatGPT data the bands sit close together: 34.3% at 500 to 999 words, 32.6% at 2,000 to 2,999, and 28.6% at 5,000 or more[7]. Add words only when they answer something.

Be careful with query fan-out. Google warns against separate content for every variation, and says that doing so mainly to manipulate rankings or AI responses "violates Google's scaled content abuse spam policy"[5]. Our broader LLM SEO playbook covers fan-out and the off-site half of the work.

How do you rewrite a page for extraction?

Work section by section, keep the facts, and change the order and the phrasing. This is the sequence we use. The evidence for each step is as rated above, and no study has tested the sequence as a whole.

  1. List the questions the page should answer, and make each one a heading in the buyer's words.
  2. Move the answer to the first sentence under each heading. If the section has no answer, cut it or find one.
  3. Read each section alone. Replace pronouns and back-references with the named subject.
  4. Date and source every number. Cut what you cannot source.
  5. Convert side-by-side prose into a table and sequences into numbered steps.
  6. Check the rendered HTML. Key facts should be present without JavaScript, outside images and PDFs, and not only in schema.
  7. Measure with repeated runs against pages you left alone, because single checks are noise.

This page follows the same pattern. That proves nothing on its own, and we will not claim a result we have not measured. To see which of your pages engines cite today before rewriting anything, request a free AI visibility audit.

faq.a: LLM optimization is the work of getting your content retrieved and cited in answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI features. At page level it means self-contained sections, answers in the first sentence, sourced numbers and key facts in visible HTML. People also call it LLM SEO or GEO. The evidence is mostly observational, so treat any promised uplift with suspicion.

faq.q: How do I optimize content for LLMs without rewriting my whole site?
faq.a: Start with the five pages that matter most commercially. Put a standalone answer at the top, phrase headings as buyer questions, answer each one in its first sentence, and turn comparisons into real HTML tables. Keep five similar pages unchanged as a rough comparison, then measure both groups with repeated prompt runs. That is not a controlled trial, but it beats a single before and after.

faq.q: Should I add FAQ schema to get cited by AI?
faq.a: Do not add it for that reason alone. Ahrefs' May 2026 test of 1,885 pages found no major citation uplift from adding JSON-LD, though it only covered pages already cited often and pooled schema types. AirOps reports a 45.6% citation rate for FAQPage pages, but that is an uncontrolled comparison. Write visible questions and answers for readers, and treat the markup as a bonus for rich results.

faq.q: Is there an ideal chunk size or word count for AI search?
faq.a: Nobody has shown one. We found no engine that publishes its chunk size as of November 2026, and Google says there is no ideal page length. Ahrefs found a near-zero correlation of 0.04 between word count and citation position in AI Overviews in December 2025. Write sections that are complete on their own, at whatever length the question needs.
